content: 1. Dr. Elizabeth Harauz is affiliated with McGill University and contributed to the evidence reviews conducted for these guidelines. 2. In patients with rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) or multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), the effectiveness of individual drugs in treatment regimens is evaluated based on specific outcomes, including cure, treatment completion, culture conversion by six months, treatment failure, relapse, survival, and adverse reactions. 3. The population includes patients with RR-TB, MDR-TB without resistance or severe intolerance to second-line drugs, MDR-TB with resistance or severe intolerance to specific drug classes (e.g., fluoroquinolones, second-line injectable drugs, pyrazinamide, or Group 4 drugs), and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) with or without additional resistance. Subpopulations include children (0–4 years, 5–14 years), persons with HIV, pregnant women, and individuals with diabetes. 4. Second-line regimens may include or exclude specific drugs such as pyrazinamide, injectable agents (kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin), prothionamide/ethionamide, cycloserine/terizidone, para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), later-generation fluoroquinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin, high-dose levofloxacin), high-dose isoniazid, clofazimine, linezolid, bedaquiline, delamanid, and other Group 5 drugs. 5. Group 4 drugs include ethionamide, prothionamide, cycloserine, terizidone, and PAS. Group 5 drugs include amoxicillin-clavulanate, bedaquiline, clarithromycin, clofazimine, delamanid, high-dose isoniazid, imipenem-cilastatin, linezolid, meropenem, and thioacetazone. 6. Definitive recommendations for the use of bedaquiline and delamanid in treatment will only be possible after the results of Phase III clinical trials become available. 7. Data from regimens lasting up to 12 months are excluded from this question and addressed in Question 3. 8. Later-generation fluoroquinolones, such as moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin, may be included in the analysis, with high-dose levofloxacin results to be reported separately. 9. In patients with drug-resistant TB patterns other than rifampicin resistance or multidrug resistance, the composition and duration of drug regimens are assessed for their likelihood to achieve outcomes such as cure, culture conversion, treatment failure, relapse, survival, adverse reactions, and acquisition of additional drug resistance. 10. Regimens for isoniazid-resistant TB may include combinations such as RZE + fluoroquinolone for 6–9 months, HRZE for 6–9 months, or other regimens. The effects are stratified by subpopulations, including children, persons with HIV, pregnant women, and individuals with diabetes. 11. The assessment of evidence and recommendations for these resistance patterns is influenced by the reliability of drug susceptibility testing (DST) for ethambutol and pyrazinamide, which is often unreliable. However, reliable DST for pyrazinamide may be available in some settings. 12. In MDR-TB patients, treatment regimens lasting up to 12 months are compared to those recommended in the 2011 WHO guidelines. These regimens typically include at least four effective second-line drugs plus pyrazinamide, with injectable agents used for 4–6 months and total treatment lasting at least 18 months after culture conversion. 13. The outcomes assessed include cure, culture conversion by six months, treatment failure, relapse, survival, adverse reactions, acquisition of additional drug resistance, and adherence to treatment. 14. Among MDR-TB patients, the impact of delayed treatment initiation and elective surgery on outcomes is evaluated. Early treatment initiation within four weeks of diagnosis is compared to delayed treatment beyond four weeks. 15. Elective surgery is assessed for its role in improving outcomes in MDR-TB and XDR-TB patients, with particular attention to subpopulations such as children, persons with HIV on antiretrovirals, pregnant women, and individuals with diabetes.
